China launches new satellite group for commercial constellation

content.text:
Assuming you mean **the first artificial satellite vs. a modern/latest satellite**, here’s a quick comparison.

| Feature | **First satellite: Sputnik 1** | **Modern/latest satellites** |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch date** | October 4, 1957 | New satellites are launched almost every week; for example, China launched a new Spacesail constellation satellite group on June 5, 2026. |
| **Country/operator** | Soviet Union | Many countries and companies: SpaceX, China, ESA, NASA, Amazon, OneWeb, etc. |
| **Size & mass** | 58 cm diameter, 83.6 kg — about beach-ball sized | Ranges from tiny CubeSats under 10 kg to multi-ton satellites |
| **Main purpose** | Proved that humans could put an object into Earth orbit; sent simple radio “beeps” | Internet, GPS/navigation, weather, Earth imaging, climate monitoring, military, science, communications |
| **Power** | Batteries only | Solar panels + batteries, often lasting years |
| **Technology** | Very simple radio transmitter | Computers, cameras, sensors, AI/automation, laser links, electric propulsion |
| **Orbit time** | About 98 minutes per orbit | Depends on orbit; many LEO satellites orbit in ~90–120 minutes |
| **Lifespan** | About 3 months in orbit; radio worked ~3 weeks | Often 5–15+ years, depending on design |
| **Communication** | Simple radio signal | High-speed data, broadband internet, encrypted links, inter-satellite laser communication |
| **Impact** | Started the Space Age and the Space Race | Supports daily life: maps, phones, banking time sync, weather forecasts, internet, disaster response |

**In short:** Sputnik 1 was a simple metal sphere that proved orbit was possible. Modern satellites are sophisticated space computers that provide internet, navigation, imaging, science data, and global communications. NASA describes Sputnik 1 as the world’s first artificial satellite, weighing **83.6 kg** and orbiting Earth in about **98 minutes**. ([nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov/history/dawn-of-the-space-age/?utm_source=openai)) Modern launches are now routine; for example, a Long March-8 launched another batch for China’s Spacesail commercial constellation on **June 5, 2026**. ([english.news.cn](https://english.news.cn/asiapacific/20260606/5fd9a871827548cc93babbea98af5d2b/c.html?utm_source=openai))
